title: Dichotic Listening and Selection Theories
summary: Follow one of two competing word streams and ignore the other, then answer two questions about what you took in. Early and late selection accounts disagree about what your answers should be.
learningObjectives: Distinguish detection of a physical change in an ignored channel from identification of its meaning.
Describe what happens to both when the attended task is made harder.
Explain which findings early selection, attenuation and late selection were each built to handle.
Explain why failure to report is weak evidence for absence of processing.
Recognise why a theory that absorbs every finding is not thereby supported by them.
interactionTypes: run with results withheld until the end
optional synthesised stereo audio with a full transcript
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; trial responses stay in the browser tab as JavaScript variables and disappear on reload, and nothing is written to storage. The optional tones are generated by oscillators in the page and involve no audio files and no network request.
accessibilityNotes: Items change once every 800 ms - about 1.25 changes a second, well below the three-per-second threshold associated with photosensitive reactions - and only the two words change; the panels, their size and their position stay put. No CSS animation or transition is used anywhere, so there is nothing for a reduced-motion setting to switch off. The attended side is marked three ways at once: a heavier border, a filled label reading Attend to this, and a caret glyph in that label, none of which is a hue. The physically marked item is larger, bolder and underlined, again not a hue. Audio is on by default because the task is a dichotic-listening analogue, synthesised from oscillators with low gains, switchable to a visual-only alternative in one control, and preceded by a Test the sound button for a headphone check; every trial is followed by a full transcript of both streams, which is the text alternative for both the visual stream and the tones. The live stream area is aria-hidden while running because reading both sides aloud would defeat the selection the task is about. Responses are by pointer or the space bar, which is captured only while a trial is running so it neither scrolls the page nor interferes with keyboard activation of other controls, with targets at least 3.25rem tall, and no trial is timed out at the response end. The chart is aria-hidden and paired inside the same figure with a five-column table; its two series differ by fill, by a hatch and by the printed value. Every control has an accessible name, headings do not skip, focus moves to the results heading, and forced-colours rules are supplied for the stream panels and both chart series. Usable at 320px and at projector widths with no horizontal page scroll; wide tables scroll inside their own containers.
readmeTopic: Selective attention: what gets through from an ignored channel, and which theory each finding troubles
simulationNotes: The learner's own trials are real responses, not simulated. A trial is 16 item pairs at 800 ms; the probe sits at pair 9, 10 or 11 and varies on two factors, marked or plain and relevant (an animal, the monitored category) or unrelated. A run is four trials, one per probe type. The attended-task rule is the load manipulation: press for every animal, or press for every animal except birds. The attended item at the probe position is always a non-target, so attended load at that moment is constant across trials. Recognition offers the probe plus five foils drawn from pools disjoint from both streams, always two animals and four non-animals so the option set never gives the answer away. Only the learner's first trial is naive; the tool reports it separately and says why. The worked example is a simulated class of 40 fictional participants with one trial per cell, mulberry32 seed 20260955, drawn as Bernoulli trials: looked different .88 and .72 for marked items under one and two rules, .17 and .10 for plain items; word recognised .62/.38, .55/.30, .34/.14 and .13/.06 for marked-relevant, marked-unrelated, plain-relevant and plain-unrelated. The two questions are drawn independently in the generator, which is a deliberate simplification - in real data they would be correlated, and the simulated plain-relevant cell accordingly shows recognition above noticing. That pattern is built in to illustrate the shape of the classic findings; it is not evidence for them, not a norm, and not anybody's data. The whole task is a visual analogue: written columns are not two spoken messages at two ears, and the tones carry separation but no words.
